problem: Prior language-guided robot navigation assumes the human guide knows the goal and gives perfect directions. Real people (e.g. in malls) are unsure and give vague or wrong directions, and robots have no way to judge how far to trust them.
motivation: Human wayfinding is error-prone and spatial anxiety makes spoken directions unreliable. A robot that blindly follows them wastes time or fails, while one that distrusts everyone over-interacts. The best degree of trust depends on the environment (office vs. mall), so the robot should learn it.
key_idea: Extract verbal affective cues (speech repair, hesitation, uncertainty words) into a per-symbol human trust metric tau_h, and train a PPO policy that also outputs a robot trust metric tau_r, rewarded for matching the environment's average tau_h, so it learns when to follow human guidance.
insight: The social reward that penalizes |tau_h - tau_r| is what keeps the robot from being purely gullible. In reward design, a high follow-reward alone made the robot gullible and ignore tau_h, and a high interaction reward made it interact at every step. In simulation the learned tau_r converges to about 0.5, the environment's average tau_h, while random exploration does not converge. Evidence is only reward and tau_r curves, with no navigation benchmark metrics.
method: Lang2Sym symbolization: a rule-based symbolizer converts spoken directions into symbols U/D/L/R; a dataset of 200+ instructions is released.
Human trust metric tau_h: probabilistic scores from speech repair (0.75), hesitation (0.5) and language uncertainty (0.5), multiplied into A_net and averaged over symbols.
Human simulation: each simulated human has a mental-map graph of gateway nodes with possibly wrong goal neighbours, and tau_h drawn from a 2D Gaussian around the goal.

Event-triggered PPO policy: an MLP whose state is triggered at gateways or human detections. Observation is {S, tau_h, N_I, N_G, D_h, D_t}; action is {L,R,U,D,I} x 10 discretized tau_r values (flattened to 50).
Reward: interaction penalty, target reward, gateway delay penalty and social reward (r_follow + r_trust, with r_trust = -w|tau_h - tau_r|), which shapes gullible vs. skeptical personality.
Real-robot transfer: object detector for people, distance-based gateway detection, and tau_h estimated from real speech affects.

setting.backbone: PPO policy with MLP (trained from scratch); rule-based symbolizer and off-the-shelf speech disfluency detector
setting.training_data: Simulated corridor environments with randomly generated virtual humans; 10K training steps, 15-step episodes; Lang2Sym dataset of 200+ instructions
setting.observation: Symbolized language guidance plus confidence scores, interaction and gateway counts, human and target detection flags; simulated 2D Lidar and RGBD for detection
setting.action_space: Discrete: reactive directions {L,R,U,D} plus interact, combined with tau_r in 10 discrete levels
setting.simulator: Custom corridor simulator with low-poly cuboid humans
setting.privileged: none at test time; the simulated humans use a mental map of the goal

numbers_note: No standard benchmark metrics. Results are only reward and tau_r curves in figures (max reward about 5K in 10K steps, tau_r converges around 0.5) and qualitative real-world comparisons.
results: In simulation the trained policy reaches a reward of about 5K within 10K steps, well above random exploration, and its tau_r converges to about 0.5, the average tau_h of the environment. Real-robot lab experiments compare skeptical and gullible models under trusty and non-trusty human directions, but no quantitative numbers are given.
limitations: Relies on noisy audio cues for disfluency, which can produce incorrect trust estimates.
Evaluation is thin: simulated corridor reward curves and a qualitative lab experiment, with no standard benchmarks or quantitative baselines.
Human behavior is simulated with hand-set affect probabilities and a Gaussian; only four direction symbols and simple gateway topology are supported.
builds_on: Language symbol abstractions (Gopalan et al., Sriram et al.)
